title: Changing-Look Black Hole Brightens Four Years Running: Its Unusual Spectrum Could Test How Spinning Black Holes Ignite
excerpt: Four-year brightening of changing-look black hole AT2022aamy confirmed. Its unusual spectrum may be first real-time test of black hole spin theory.
content:
Deep inside a distant galaxy, a supermassive black hole that was silent in every archival spectrum has been waking up — and it has not stopped. New photometric measurements in The Astronomer's Telegram confirm that AT2022aamy, one of the most closely watched "changing-look" black holes discovered in the past decade, has brightened again: reaching g = 17.05, r = 16.17, and i = 15.61 magnitudes as of this morning, compared to a g-band reading of 17.21 recorded about 381 days ago by the Zwicky Transient Facility. The object has been brightening continuously since it was first catalogued in 2022 — a four-year arc of ignition playing out on a timescale humans can actually watch.

What makes this particular black hole scientifically extraordinary is not just that it is brightening. It is how it is brightening — and what the shape of its light reveals about the machine running underneath.

What Is a "Changing-Look" Black Hole, and Why Does It Matter to You?

For most of the history of observational astronomy, astronomers treated active galactic nuclei — the blazingly luminous cores of galaxies powered by gas falling into supermassive black holes — as essentially stable objects. A nucleus either showed broad emission lines (gas moving at thousands of miles per second around the black hole, labeled "Type 1") or it did not (labeled "Type 2"). The prevailing explanation was geometric: Type 2 nuclei were simply Type 1s seen edge-on, with the inner regions hidden behind a doughnut-shaped curtain of dust. The black hole had not changed; the view had.

Changing-look AGN — CLAGNs, in the literature — broke that model. These are galactic nuclei whose broad emission lines appear or disappear on timescales of months to years — timescales so short that no motion of a dust torus could explain them. The changing is real. The black hole itself is switching states.

Astronomers now recognize two distinct flavors of changing-look event. In the first, a column of gas and dust drifts across the line of sight, temporarily screening the inner region — variable obscuration. In the second, more fundamental category, the accretion flow itself changes: the black hole eats more (or less), the disk heats up (or cools down), and the ultraviolet and X-ray radiation that "lights up" the surrounding gas cloud either floods the region or vanishes. AT2022aamy belongs to this second, rarer, more revealing category — a turn-on event, in which broad emission lines absent from every earlier spectrum have emerged with real strength over the past four years.

This matters beyond academic astronomy. Supermassive black holes — ranging from a million to several billion times the mass of the Sun — sit at the center of nearly every large galaxy, including our own Milky Way. How they transition between dormant and active states shapes the galaxies around them: AGN feedback drives outflows that heat gas, suppress star formation, and regulate the structure of the universe at large. Understanding what flips the switch is not a minor footnote. It is a central question in our understanding of how the cosmos evolves.

The Double-Peaked Smoking Gun

What sets AT2022aamy apart from other brightening black holes is the specific shape of its newly emerged emission lines.

When the Transient Name Server first flagged this object, the spectrum showed something unusual: double-peaked broad H-alpha and H-beta emission lines — a profile with two distinct humps rather than a single broad mound. That shape is not generic. It carries a precise physical meaning.

In a simplified picture of an accretion disk, gas on one side of the disk is moving toward us (blueshifted) while gas on the opposite side is receding (redshifted). When the emission comes directly from the outer disk itself — rather than from a diffuse cloud of gas far removed from the disk plane — both Doppler-shifted populations produce light simultaneously, and the combined profile shows the characteristic twin-peaked structure. Studies of such profiles in SDSS-selected AGN have confirmed they are consistent with accretion disks viewed at inclinations below roughly 50 degrees, with emissivity patterns consistent with photoionized disk atmospheres.

Crucially, the double-peaked structure also carries information about the black hole's current feeding state. Research into strongly variable AGN has shown that broad-line profiles tend to show double-peak morphology in the low-Eddington-ratio regime — when the black hole is feeding well below its theoretical maximum rate — and transition toward a single-peaked profile as the feeding rate rises. Seeing a double-peaked profile emerge during the early stages of a turn-on event tells astronomers that the emission is coming from the outer accretion disk itself, not from a spherical halo of gas, and that the disk is at an inclination where both approaching and receding sides are visible.

Here is where the story gets genuinely exciting — and where this observation may point toward something much larger.

A theoretical paper published earlier this year proposed that at least some changing-look events are driven not by a gradual increase in the accretion rate, but by a process called disk tearing: when a tilted accretion disk orbits a rapidly spinning black hole, the black hole's rotation distorts spacetime around it (a phenomenon called Lense-Thirring precession, or frame dragging), torquing the inner and outer disk at different rates until the disk literally tears apart into discrete, independently precessing rings. These rings collide, cancel angular momentum, and dump material onto the black hole in sudden surges — producing order-of-magnitude swings in luminosity on the same months-to-years timescales seen in changing-look events.

The disk-tearing model makes a specific, testable prediction: as the independent rings precess at different rates, the BLR illumination pattern rotates, and the red and blue peaks of a double-peaked emission line should show evolving asymmetries — the red peak brightening relative to the blue, or vice versa, over weeks to months as the geometry shifts.

AT2022aamy, with its double-peaked Balmer profile emerging during an active brightening phase, is now a live candidate for exactly this test. If spectroscopic follow-up over the coming months reveals a time-varying red-to-blue asymmetry in the double-peaked profile, it would be the first real-time observational fingerprint of disk tearing as a CLAGN driver — and potentially the most direct evidence yet that the Lense-Thirring effect is shaping how supermassive black holes turn on.

The double-peaked profile is not merely a marker of disk geometry. It is specifically the shape a disk-tearing scenario predicts will evolve asymmetrically, making it a potential discriminator between models in a way that total brightness alone cannot achieve.

China's World-Class New Observatory Is Watching

The new measurements that prompted today's alert were carried out by researchers Bing Lyu, Ruixiang Hu, and Bei You of Wuhan University, using an instrument called MATCH — the Multi-mode Autonomous Terminal for Compatible Hybrid-optics — mounted on the Wuhan University 1-meter optical telescope.

MATCH is equipped with a large-format QHY411 CMOS camera: a 14,304 × 10,748 pixel array with 3.76-micrometer pixels, actively cooled to –30°C (–22°F). That deep cooling delivers readout noise of just 1.0 to 3.0 electrons per pixel and a dark current of only 0.0011 electrons per pixel per second — noise characteristics that make precise differential photometry of faint nuclear transients possible even against the bright background glow of a host galaxy.

That host-galaxy background is exactly what makes this measurement technically demanding. To isolate the light coming specifically from the black hole rather than from the surrounding galaxy's stars, the team employed image-subtraction photometry: subtracting a reference image of the galaxy's starlight from the new frame, leaving behind only the variable nuclear emission. The two columns in today's photometry table — differential magnitude and image-subtraction magnitude — represent two independent ways of quantifying the same brightening:

BandMJDDifferential MagnitudeImage-Subtraction Magnitude
g61350.62917.048 ± 0.02616.855 ± 0.077
r61350.63016.171 ± 0.01516.211 ± 0.045
i61350.63115.612 ± 0.02715.697 ± 0.035

MJD = Modified Julian Date, an astronomical timekeeping convention. MJD 61350 corresponds to November 7, 2026.

The g-band value of 17.05 is notably brighter than the ZTF reference measurement of 17.21 ± 0.02 mag from approximately 381 days earlier — a brightening of roughly 0.16 magnitudes in g-band. The r- and i-band readings (16.17 and 15.61, respectively) indicate an increasingly red spectral slope consistent with growing thermal emission from hot accreting gas.

The telescope's home — the Lenghu Observatory on Saishiteng Mountain in Qinghai Province, China — is one of the most consequential emerging astronomical sites in the world. Perched at 4,200 to 4,500 meters (13,800 to 14,800 feet) above sea level on the Tibetan Plateau, Lenghu was assessed in a three-year study in Nature as being on par with the world's premier observing sites, including Cerro Paranal in Chile and Mauna Kea in Hawaii. Its median seeing of approximately 0.75 arcseconds (a measure of atmospheric blurring), its approximately 70% fraction of photometric nights, and its precipitable water vapor below 2 millimeters on more than half of all nights place it among the best in the world for high-precision optical astronomy.

Critically, Lenghu sits at a longitude — roughly 93°E — that fills a gap in the global network of elite observatories. When Mauna Kea goes dark at dawn and European sites have not yet reached night, Lenghu can keep watching. For a slowly evolving transient like AT2022aamy, that continuous longitudinal coverage is not incidental. It is the difference between catching a spectral evolution over days and missing it.

Why This Brightening Is Happening: Three Competing Theories

The physical mechanism behind turn-on CLAGN events remains one of the most contested problems in observational high-energy astrophysics. Three frameworks are currently competing in the literature.

The accretion-rate model is the most intuitive. Sudden increases in the mass flow reaching the central black hole push the inner accretion disk inward, dramatically increasing the production of ionizing ultraviolet and X-ray photons — the specific radiation that excites the BLR into emitting bright broad lines. Research linking X-ray luminosity and broad-line flux in CLAGNs supports a picture where the system occupies a critical transition zone near a bolometric Eddington ratio of roughly 1%, where even modest changes in mass flow produce large changes in BLR emission. Work on ZTF18abuamgo — a comparable changing-look AGN studied this year in MNRAS — directly confirmed this picture: the Type 1.5 to Type 1.2 transition over approximately four years was driven by a rise in Eddington ratio from 0.032 to 0.08, with no significant change in obscuration. Broad-line region electron temperatures around 11,800–11,900 K were measured at peak — a data point now within reach for AT2022aamy through its rising Balmer emission.

The accretion-mode transition model goes one step deeper. When the accretion rate rises above a critical threshold — typically near 1% of the Eddington rate — the inner disk can transition from a radiatively inefficient, geometrically thick "advection-dominated accretion flow" (ADAF) to a geometrically thin, optically thick disk. In the ADAF state, most of the energy released by infalling gas is swallowed by the black hole rather than radiated away; the BLR sees almost no ionizing photons and stays dark. The transition to a thin disk floods the system with UV and soft X-ray radiation, switching the BLR on. Work from the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory has proposed that size variability of the inner ADAF disk naturally produces the observed changing-look transitions, with the ADAF contracting as the accretion rate climbs.

The disk-tearing model offers the most radical explanation — and, with AT2022aamy's double-peaked profile in hand, the most testable. As described above, a misaligned disk around a rapidly spinning black hole can be torn by Lense-Thirring precession into independently precessing rings, producing sudden luminosity surges on timescales far shorter than the standard viscous timescale. Unlike the first two models, disk tearing predicts not just a brightening but a specific spectral asymmetry in double-peaked broad lines — a time-varying imbalance between the red and blue peaks as the geometry of the torn disk evolves.

For AT2022aamy specifically, the absence of significant X-ray obscuration — if confirmed by follow-up X-ray observations — combined with the infrared continuum tracking the optical brightening, would point firmly toward intrinsic accretion changes rather than a dust screen lifting. That is consistent with both the accretion-rate and accretion-mode models. But only disk tearing predicts the evolving asymmetry. Only spectroscopy can tell them apart.

The Case for Spectroscopic Follow-Up — Now

The Wuhan University team closed their telegram with a direct appeal: "Further spectroscopic observations will continue and are encouraged." For anyone in the time-domain astronomy community, that phrasing has a specific meaning: the source is at a juncture where data taken in the next few weeks will shape how the story develops over the next few years.

What spectroscopy in the coming weeks could reveal:

  • Line profile evolution: Whether the double-peaked H-alpha and H-beta profiles are sharpening or blurring — a direct probe of disk geometry and illumination changes over time, and the critical measurement for the disk-tearing asymmetry test.
  • Reverberation lag: Whether the emission-line flux is tracking the continuum rise or lagging behind it. The lag, measurable via reverberation mapping, encodes the physical radius of the BLR: light from the central engine must travel outward to the BLR before the lines respond, so the delay in days corresponds directly to the BLR's size in light-days.
  • Higher-ionization species: Whether lines like He II λ4686 or [Fe VII] are beginning to emerge — a signal that the central engine has become hot enough to photoionize more exotic gas, constraining the spectral energy distribution of the driving radiation.
  • BLR temperature: Applying the Boltzmann plot method to the visible Balmer series, as done for ZTF18abuamgo this year, can yield the BLR's electron temperature — connecting this object to the growing empirical sample of well-characterized CLAGNs.

Facilities suited for this follow-up include the Kast Spectrograph at Lick Observatory, ESO's VLT/X-Shooter, the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph, and the LAMOST survey telescope — the latter already deployed for systematic CLAGN monitoring in the northern sky. Even small robotic telescopes with low-resolution spectrographs can contribute to tracking evolving line profiles over time.

A Black Hole in a Wider Context

AT2022aamy joins an increasingly well-monitored registry of CLAGNs being tracked by both targeted follow-up and all-sky survey platforms.

The Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), operating from the 48-inch Samuel Oschin Schmidt Telescope at Palomar Observatory, California, has become the backbone of the community's ability to catch nuclear transients in the act. Its 576-megapixel camera covers 47 square degrees of sky per exposure — roughly 90 times the area of the full Moon — and scans the entire northern sky every two to three days to limiting magnitudes of approximately g~20.8. That dense time-domain baseline makes it the natural reference against which targeted follow-up measurements, like today's from Lenghu, are compared.

Statistical surveys have begun to characterize CLAGNs as a population. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey V (SDSS-V) CLAGN sample — one of the largest assembled to date — found that roughly 67% of CLAGNs dim while approximately 33% brighten, with a clear preference for low Eddington ratios in the transitioning objects. If changing-look transitions occur in 10% to 20% of AGN over cosmic time, as some estimates suggest, then this is not a curiosity. It is a standard chapter in the life of a supermassive black hole — one that most of them go through, that shapes their host galaxies, and that plays out on timescales short enough for astronomers to watch from start to finish.

AT2022aamy's object designation follows the IAU transient naming convention: the year prefix indicates it was first catalogued in 2022, meaning this brightening arc has been evolving for roughly four years before today's latest measurement. If the trend holds, it may become one of the best-studied slow-rise turn-on CLAGNs in the literature — a long, well-sampled light curve spanning the full arc of AGN ignition.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a changing-look AGN?

A changing-look active galactic nucleus is a galactic core powered by a supermassive black hole whose spectral appearance changes dramatically over timescales of months to years — specifically, one in which the broad emission lines from fast-moving gas around the black hole appear or disappear. This contradicts the classic model that said AGN types were fixed by viewing angle, and suggests instead that the black hole's accretion flow itself can switch states on observable timescales.

What does the double-peaked emission line profile tell us?

A double-peaked broad emission line profile means the light is coming from two distinct populations of gas moving in opposite directions around the black hole — the approaching and receding sides of the accretion disk — producing a twin-humped spectral shape rather than a single broad peak. This is a marker of emission arising directly from the outer accretion disk, at a relatively low Eddington ratio (the black hole is feeding below its theoretical maximum rate). It is also the specific spectral shape that disk-tearing models predict will evolve asymmetrically over time, making it a discriminating test for competing theories.

What is MJD?

MJD stands for Modified Julian Date, a continuous count of days used by astronomers to avoid ambiguities in calendar dates across time zones. MJD 61350 corresponds to November 7, 2026. The photometry table reports measurements taken at MJD 61350.629–61350.631, meaning within about 15 minutes of each other on the morning of November 7.

Where is the Lenghu Observatory?

Lenghu Observatory is located on Saishiteng Mountain in Qinghai Province, China — on the Tibetan Plateau at an elevation of approximately 4,200 to 4,500 meters (13,800 to 14,800 feet) above sea level. A three-year site characterization published in Nature found its atmospheric conditions comparable to the world's premier observatories. Its location in the Eastern Hemisphere fills a longitudinal gap in global time-domain observing coverage.

What is the Zwicky Transient Facility?

ZTF is a wide-field sky survey operating from the 48-inch Samuel Oschin Schmidt Telescope at Palomar Observatory in California. Its camera covers 47 square degrees per exposure and scans the entire northern sky every two to three days. It is the primary survey instrument detecting and tracking transient events like AT2022aamy, and its measurements provide the baseline against which follow-up observations are compared.

Can amateur astronomers observe AT2022aamy?

AT2022aamy is currently around magnitude 15.6 to 17.1 depending on the band — well within reach of a 10-inch or larger telescope under dark skies with a sensitive camera. However, the scientifically valuable measurements at this stage are spectroscopic (measuring the shape and asymmetry of emission lines), which require a telescope-and-spectrograph combination beyond most amateur setups. Photometric brightness monitoring — tracking how bright the nucleus is over time — can be contributed by well-equipped amateurs with access to calibrated photometry workflows.

What Comes Next

The broader theoretical prize on offer is understanding how a supermassive black hole transitions between its "off" and "on" states on human-observable timescales, and whether the double-peaked disk-emission signature encoded in AT2022aamy's spectrum can help discriminate between three models — disk instability, accretion-mode transition, and disk tearing — that are actively contending for primacy in the literature.

The disk-tearing model's prediction of evolving red-to-blue asymmetry in the double-peaked profile is the most specific, the most falsifiable, and the most consequential. If that asymmetry is detected in spectroscopic follow-up over the next weeks and months, it would not merely confirm one model over another. It would provide the first direct, real-time observational evidence that Lense-Thirring frame dragging — the warping of spacetime by a spinning black hole, a prediction of general relativity — is shaping the structure of an accretion disk in a specific, measurable, astronomical-scale way.

As the MATCH team continues its photometric monitoring from the pristine, high-altitude skies of the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, the global AGN community has been put on notice. A black hole that has been waking up for four years is now entering what may be its most informative phase. The science of watching it happen in real time is only just beginning.
